cells.tense: What you're going after and what you're feeling are lined up right now.
cells.ask: Before the next step, say out loud which feeling it's coming from. One minute, and that's it.
cells.core:
You know what you're headed for, and you know why. Not because you argued yourself into it — because the aim came out of something you felt, and it stayed. So when you move, you move from the middle of yourself, and people around you can tell. You're not pushing and you're not coasting.

This is easy to miss while you're in it. The direction is doing its job without drama. If you stopped and checked, you'd find the aim and the feeling were not separate in the first place. That's worth noticing now, because noticing it is what lets you keep it.
cells.sheetLine: You're moving, and it's coming from something real.
cells.place: where other people are the ground you stand on

cells.tense: You're racing toward a finish line that keeps moving further out in front of you.
cells.ask: Take two minutes off the next step. Not forever — just long enough to say whether you still want what you're chasing.
cells.core:
The momentum is real. The problem is that arriving stopped being the point somewhere along the way. You get close, the target shifts, and you take that as a signal to push harder rather than a signal to look. You're not confused about where you're going. You're just not arriving.

The feeling underneath is still there too. It's being spent as fuel instead of read as direction, and you can tell, because when you picture getting there, what you imagine is being allowed to stop. That's not the same as wanting the thing. Worth a pause before the next push.

cells.tense: You felt a pull toward something and you've been standing at the doorway since.
cells.ask: Say one sentence to one person about what you'd go toward if nothing went wrong. It doesn't have to be true. Just once, out loud.
cells.core:
The feeling is still here. It's been here a while — toward someone, or some way of spending your days that isn't this one. You haven't stepped, and you haven't said no either. Saying either way would settle something, so it stays unsettled. Done well, that pull has somewhere to land: it becomes a plan someone else has heard, and moving stops being a private argument you keep losing. Yours has no outlet and no witness.

People read this as you being fine where you are. You're not numb. You can feel the gap between what you're doing and what you'd choose. The pull hasn't left. It's parked.
cells.sheetLine: You felt the pull, and you've been standing still.

cells.tense: You're steering something and calling it the way things had to go.
cells.ask: Name one choice from this week you've been calling 'what was needed.' Say it was yours, out loud, once.
cells.core:
You move. That part isn't in doubt. What's less clear is whether you know it's you doing the moving. Here's how it shows: you decide something, you act, and by the time it comes up in conversation it's been filed under logistics — what had to happen, what the week required. The feeling that led to it doesn't get mentioned.

This isn't modesty and it isn't a lie. It's that what you wanted doesn't count as a reason in your own bookkeeping. So the direction is real and the one who chose it is standing right there, uncredited. Saying it plainly wouldn't make you softer. It would just put the choice back where it started.
cells.sheetLine: You're moving. You just haven't claimed it.
